Limitations
URGen assumes that a ﬂatter keypoint-ranking dis-
tribution warrants more context. It may fail when
the model is consistently conﬁdent about wrong or
incomplete keypoints: ZARD can then assign low
entropy, shrink the context, and miss necessary ev-
idence. Appendix Table S10 quantiﬁes this failure
mode: 2 of 26 errors occur in the lowest uncer-
tainty quartile and 5 of 51 in the lower half. These
counts do not directly establish ranking correct-
ness because gold keypoint labels are unavailable.
URGen also cannot recover evidence absent from
its corpus. Our evaluation uses complete disease-
scoped galleries of 35 TED or 22 GD keypoints;
the pooled-gallery test in Appendix Table S8 adds
disease-speciﬁc distractors but does not establish
robustness for web-scale retrieval or automatically
extracted, noisy corpora.
Computationally, URGen’s multi-temperature
ranking and answer aggregation increase total in-
ference work.
Appendix Table S3 reports 4.33
GPU-s/question, above Fixed-1 (3.78) but below
Fixed-5 (5.48); batching independent branches
does not remove this total-compute cost. Finally,
the present evidence is limited to multiple-choice
ophthalmology QA with authoritative guidelines.
Applying URGen to other specialties requires a
new veriﬁed corpus, and its behavior for open-
ended tasks remains untested.

Limitations
URGen assumes that a ﬂatter keypoint-ranking dis-
tribution warrants more context. It may fail when
the model is consistently conﬁdent about wrong or
incomplete keypoints: ZARD can then assign low
entropy, shrink the context, and miss necessary ev-
idence. Appendix Table S10 quantiﬁes this failure
mode: 2 of 26 errors occur in the lowest uncer-
tainty quartile and 5 of 51 in the lower half. These
counts do not directly establish ranking correct-
ness because gold keypoint labels are unavailable.
URGen also cannot recover evidence absent from
its corpus. Our evaluation uses complete disease-
scoped galleries of 35 TED or 22 GD keypoints;
the pooled-gallery test in Appendix Table S8 adds
disease-speciﬁc distractors but does not establish
robustness for web-scale retrieval or automatically
extracted, noisy corpora.
Computationally, URGen’s multi-temperature
ranking and answer aggregation increase total in-
ference work. Appendix Table S3 reports 4.33
GPU-s/question, above Fixed-1 (3.78) but below
Fixed-5 (5.48); batching independent branches
does not remove this total-compute cost. Finally,
the present evidence is limited to multiple-choice
ophthalmology QA with authoritative guidelines.
Applying URGen to other specialties requires a
new veriﬁed corpus, and its behavior for open-
ended tasks remains untested.

Dataset overview.
We construct two expert-

benchmark is based on the Management of Thy-

Thyroid Associations1 (Burch et al., 2022), while

Thyroid Association Guideline for the Manage-

contraindications, referral criteria, and follow-up
guidance, all of which are important for clinically
grounded medical QA.
The resulting datasets are designed to support
several evaluation goals.

questions that require guideline-level knowledge

because every question is paired with a curated
keypoint corpus, the datasets allow controlled eval-

and evidence sufﬁciency. Third, they support relia-
bility evaluation through uncertainty metrics such
as expected calibration error (ECE) and overcon-
ﬁdent error rate (OC@0.8). Finally, they can be
used to study whether a model can avoid noisy
or redundant context when multiple clinically re-
lated but answer-irrelevant guideline statements
are available.

options, a gold option label, and the corresponding
topic-speciﬁc keypoint corpus. The questions are
written to test clinically meaningful distinctions,

E
Uncertainty Analysis
Relation to semantic graph uncertainty.
Free-
form uncertainty metrics such as Deg, Ecc, EigV,
and word-sequence entropy (Lin et al., 2024) esti-
mate uncertainty from the lexical or semantic di-
versity of multiple generated answers. They are
most informative when generations are long and
can form multiple semantic clusters. Our task is
a constrained multiple-choice setting: each gener-
ation contains a discrete option choice and a short
rationale.
Under this format, Jaccard- or NLI-
based similarity graphs are dominated by whether
two outputs select the same option, so these graph-
based metrics largely reduce to functions of the op-
tion vote distribution.
Why answer entropy alone is insufﬁcient?
The main-paper ablation already isolates this ef-
fect: replacing fused uncertainty with answer en-
tropy only leaves the ﬁnal predictions unchanged
but worsens OC@0.8 from 1.98% to 6.93% and
ECE from 6.80% to 12.31%.
This shows that
disagreement among generated options is not suf-
ﬁcient for reliable calibration; context ambiguity
must also be modeled. In clinical QA, a model
can repeatedly emit the same answer while re-
lying on an incomplete or mismatched keypoint
set.
URGen therefore combines answer uncer-
tainty with context uncertainty derived from the
keypoint ranking distribution.

Interpretation of context uncertainty.
Context
uncertainty should not be interpreted as a direct
measure of disease uncertainty.
It measures in-
stability in the retrieved keypoint distribution. A
high context-uncertainty score indicates that mul-
tiple keypoints are similarly plausible for the ques-
tion, which may reﬂect broad clinical scope, miss-
ing decisive evidence, or ambiguous wording. A
low context-uncertainty score indicates that the
ranking is concentrated on a small number of key-
points. Fusing this score with answer uncertainty
makes the ﬁnal uncertainty sensitive to both re-
trieval ambiguity and answer-generation ambigu-
ity.

eventually predicts the correct option. URGen se-
lects a smaller keypoint set and produces a sub-
stantially lower uncertainty score. This comple-
ments the quantitative results by illustrating how
adaptive depth suppresses redundant context while

Interpretation of context uncertainty. Context
uncertainty should not be interpreted as a direct
measure of disease uncertainty. It measures in-
stability in the retrieved keypoint distribution. A
high context-uncertainty score indicates that mul-
tiple keypoints are similarly plausible for the ques-
tion, which may reﬂect broad clinical scope, miss-
ing decisive evidence, or ambiguous wording. A
low context-uncertainty score indicates that the
ranking is concentrated on a small number of key-
points. Fusing this score with answer uncertainty
makes the ﬁnal uncertainty sensitive to both re-
trieval ambiguity and answer-generation ambigu-
ity.
F More Case Studies
Table S13 provides an additional TED case study.
The example shows that ﬁxed-depth retrieval may
include weakly related keypoints even when it
eventually predicts the correct option. URGen se-
lects a smaller keypoint set and produces a sub-
stantially lower uncertainty score. This comple-
ments the quantitative results by illustrating how
adaptive depth suppresses redundant context while
preserving the decisive keypoints.
Case analysis. The vanilla model chooses
contrast-enhanced CT despite the guideline-
speciﬁc preference for noncontrast CT in this
surgical-planning context. Fixed-5 RAG corrects
the answer, but its uncertainty remains high be-
cause the retrieved keypoints include several broad
TED assessment and referral statements that are
only weakly related to the imaging modality. UR-
Gen retrieves a smaller set of high-ranking key-
points and assigns a lower uncertainty score to the
same correct answer. This example illustrates an
important distinction: retrieving more keypoints
can increase topical coverage, but it can also in-
troduce redundant or weakly relevant context that
makes the model less certain. URGen’s adaptive
depth selection helps balance evidence sufﬁciency
and context compactness.
Qualitative takeaway. The case study supports
the quantitative trend in the main paper. When the
keypoint distribution is concentrated, URGen con-
tracts the context and avoids unnecessary guide-
line material. When the keypoint distribution is
diffuse, the method can expand the context to re-
duce the risk of missing key clinical information.
This behavior is especially important for guideline-
grounded medical QA, where several keypoints
may be semantically close but only one or two are
clinically decisive for the ﬁnal option.
G Prompt Templates
URGen is implemented in a training-free manner
using two prompt templates. The ﬁrst prompt
ranks candidate guideline keypoints for retrieval,
and the second prompt answers the multiple-
choice question using only the selected keypoint-
passage blocks. The prompts enforce structured
JSON output to make retrieval ranking and answer
extraction reproducible.
